items.title: It never ends...
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
After talking up this summit for months on end, it ended with no real accomplishments, and certainly not with the results Trump had hoped for. He had wanted to discuss the war in Iran and nuclear weapons, but the three men left without announcing any agreement to end the fighting or reduce their nuclear arsenals. They did, however, manage to agree on something else. Trump, Xi, and Putin issued a joint declaration that called for protecting government officials from prosecution and limiting the power of the International Criminal Court, the court responsible for prosecuting some of the world’s worst crimes, including war crimes. Of all the things these three men could have agreed on, one of them was protecting government leaders from international prosecution. That is telling, although hardly surprising coming from them...
This morning, inside the Dirksen Senate Office Building, Michael LoSapio, Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is the agency responsible for helping protect American elections from cyberattacks and foreign interference, was asked a question that should have been incredibly easy to answer.  Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut wanted to know whether the United States Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021. LoSapio said no, “I don’t believe it was an attack.” When Blumenthal pushed him further, LoSapio responded by claiming, “I wasn’t involved in politics. I know what I saw on the news.” Then Blumenthal asked him who won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election. Again, LoSapio refused to acknowledge what happened. “I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” he said. The man Donald Trump wants to put in charge of the federal agency responsible for helping protect our elections refused to acknowledge that the Capitol was attacked on January 6, and then refused to say who won the popular vote in 2020. Blumenthal looked at him and said, “You are disqualified from the position that you’ve been nominated to fill.”
He was not the only one today to deny or downplay what happened on January 6. Michael Chamberlain, who Donald Trump nominated to lead the Office of Government Ethics, the people who are supposed to hold public officials accountable, was asked the same question about January 6. He called it “behavior they shouldn’t have.” But he would not call it an attack or an insurrection, or even acknowledge what actually happened that day when a mob stormed the Capitol in an attempt to overturn an election...
During a separate hearing, just the day before, this time for a lifetime appointment to the federal judiciary, James P. Sullivan, a sitting justice on the Texas Supreme Court whom Donald Trump nominated to become a federal district judge in Texas, was asked whether Donald Trump could constitutionally run for president again in 2028. Sullivan initially struggled to even remember what the Twenty-second Amendment said, and Senator Chris Coons of Delaware had to help him. As Coons explained, the Twenty-second Amendment is very clear. It says a president who has been elected twice cannot be elected again. But when Coons asked Sullivan whether that meant Trump could not run again, Sullivan would not answer and called it an ongoing political debate. Senator Chris Coons told him, “That’s a very disappointing answer.”

items.title: The autobiography of Gunhild Lien Finseth
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
Since Mathilde has asked me to write down a little of my "pilgrimage" through life, I shall try in all frailty, though I suppose there will not be much coherence to it.
I was born into this sinful world by parents Asle Eriksen Lien and wife Guri, née Jeglum, on January 23, 1847, and baptized on the 31st of the same year, in Torpo Annex, Hallingdal. On April 25, 1861, Father decided to take the children and travel to America due to unfortunate business affairs there.  God led us with His fatherly hand over to the place where we landed. We set out from Drammen on May 6 and arrived in St. Peter on July 18, where we had an uncle whom we traveled to. They lived in a small log house, and there we climbed up on a ladder, fixed up a bed on the loft, and there we had plenty of visits from mosquitoes, so we had to make a "smudge" as they called it, took some scraps of wood chips and straw, set fire to it so the smoke chased the mosquitoes away from us somewhat; yes, such guesthouses they were in those days. Not a chair, only stools and benches and the like to sit on. The three oldest of us had to go out and get work, which was not very lucrative; my oldest sister Betsy worked for an American and got 50 cents a month, and I and my younger sister Guro got 25 cents a month. I must add that I did not get a cent in cash, but got a little calico for a dress and skirt, and Mother had to take a little wool for what I had earned.
Yes, all that I did there at that time would have been a fair day's wage in the present time; yes, a maid would never have done all that I had to do. God had given me good health and strength to work both outside and inside. In September I was to get better wages with a family closer to St. Peter; they promised me 50 cents a month, and when it came down to it I got a pair of shoes and a "hood" for having worked there for 3 months. Milked the cows and worked outside.
Then I traveled home for Christmas. In the month of March I was to go to town and try to get a place there, and it succeeded; got $4 a month there.  My two sisters worked there as well. Mother and the three youngest lived out in the country about 11 miles north of St. Peter. Late in August or September [1862] the Indians broke out [the U.S.–Dakota War], so the country folk had to flee into town, leaving everything behind—both cattle, houses, and homes—and went to Sjabnee [Shakopee].  Good and well, the horses took a road southwestward; when they got as far as a mile away from our home, ours was spared from fire and destruction. My Mother decided to turn back to the little she had, and travel to Goodhue County.
Two of our friends from Norway met us in Hastings with ox teams, took us and our things to Kittel Linnergaarden. There we stayed for a whole two years; that is to say, as a home to resort to. Those of us who were of use had to go out and work for a living. We came to Goodhue in late autumn 1861 [likely meant 1862]. I got work with Ole Nose for room and board when I set out and signed up for confirmation with Pastor Muus. We met either in a farmhouse or in a schoolhouse on the east side of Valley Grove. On the third Sunday in Advent I was confirmed in the house of John Hanson west of Valley Grove. That was for me a great and solemn day, and I must give Pastor Muus all the honor for it, because he explained it so clearly and thoroughly so that it would take root.
Still, the promise was surely broken; I became far too lively and ungodly a youth, so I became just as ungodly as my companions. Yet I often felt remorse that I should behave so, with jesting and dancing, but my Catechism Explanation was always with me, and that was probably the only book I owned. Nor were there newspapers or magazines at that time.
In the winter of 1863 we were supposed to go to English school. The schoolmaster was surely not very learned; I believe a schoolchild of the 4th grade would have come much further than our teacher. We had a couple of miles to walk and the snow became too deep to get through, so all I got of English school was about three weeks. Oh dear, how I have regretted that I did not get at least one winter term.
Time and years passed; in the summer I was often at home and helped Mother to gather hay for her cows. In order to get someone to mow the hay, we had to help stack hay for them.
In the spring of 1866 I was married to Ole K. Finseth on June 7th by Pastor Muus. We lived together with Anders Finseth until autumn, October 4th, when we moved into our new house, and there we lived together until the spring of 1912, on May 18th, when the Lord took my dear husband to Himself from the struggle to eternal joy and bliss.
The Lord granted us 9 sweet children; the youngest the Lord took home to Himself at 5 years old in 1894. In the autumn of 1915 we traveled to Silverton, Oregon; the thought was to experience and find out whether the climate would be better than in Minnesota, and thought to live there 1 or 2 years, but the result became that I am here still.

items.content: It's one thing to collect and analyze and explain data, but sometimes more important is how the data is displayed.  The graphic embedded above, originally posted in The Economist, is a beautiful and effective presentation.  The trends would be way less apparent were the numbers presented in a massive table of numbers.  Kudos to the statisticians who created this.

items.title: Interesting mittens
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
"The mittens were almost 80 years old when Ethel Dougan painted this watercolor, one of more than 18,000 works by some 1,000 financially strapped artists commissioned by the Index of American Design. Part of the Works Progress Administration’s Federal Art Project, the Index aimed to document historical American arts and crafts and provide inspiration for modern designers."
The mittens were crafted in 1862 by a young woman for her fiancee.  Can you suss out the reason for the design based on the color scheme and the date?  Answer below the fold...
"The mittens had been knitted by the fiancée of Private Franklin Martin Spaulding, an 18-year-old who had enlisted in the 6th Massachusetts Volunteer Infantry Regiment in August 1862. He had seen active service through that winter, as had his mittens... Worn and faded, certainly, they are nonetheless spirited, with a , embroidered stars, and rib-stitched stripes.
Nestled between the usual two pouches—a big one for the fingers and a small one for the thumb—is a third... It’s there for the teenage soldier’s index finger, so he could tear the end off a paper cartridge, load his rifle, and pull the trigger in the cold."
After noting the cleverness and knitting skill of the young woman, lets also note the skill of the watercolor artist, who has depicted the knit pattern with such detail that another craftsperson could recognize and duplicate it.
